clue.text: In touch with a tribal conference

blocks.note: taken as written
a dab is a light touch
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone in contact with a meeting of tribal elders.
explanation.walkthrough: An indaba is a Zulu word for a gathering held to discuss important matters, used widely in southern Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: The word comes from the Zulu and Xhosa languages and names a council or meeting of tribal leaders.

clue.text: Stamps one “125 gallons” — about right

indicators.note: about means going round, so the measure surrounds the single letter

blocks.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
a thousand pints, with M the Roman numeral for a thousand and eight pints to the gallon
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Stamps marked with a capacity of one hundred and twenty-five gallons, roughly correct.
explanation.walkthrough: With eight pints to the gallon, 125 gallons is a thousand pints, and M is the Roman thousand.
explanation.definitionFit: Imprints are marks pressed into a surface, just as stamps are impressions left by a die.

clue.text: Pirate's apprentice so slavishly obedient

blocks.note: surface: a young pirate cowed by his master
setter's reading: Frederic, apprentice in The Pirates of Penzance, is subtitled the Slave of Duty

explanation.walkthrough: Gilbert and Sullivan's The Pirates of Penzance is subtitled The Slave of Duty, after Frederic, the pirates' apprentice.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone bound by a sense of duty is conscientiously obedient, like Frederic who serves the pirates out of obligation.

clue.text: Red macaroni's stolen

blocks.note: a macaroni was an 18th-century dandy, as was a blood
taken as written
hot goods are stolen ones

explanation.surface: Someone's stolen pasta, coloured red.
explanation.walkthrough: A macaroni and a blood were both fashionable young men about town in Georgian England.
explanation.definitionFit: Bloodshot eyes are reddened by swollen blood vessels, so the word describes a red appearance.

clue.text: Putting out no end of Oxford blues

indicators.note: having no end means the final letter of the following word is missing, so it is dropped from the other word

blocks.note: the final letter of Oxford
the blues means low spirits

explanation.surface: Oxford's rowing Blues being knocked out, with no end of gloom.
explanation.walkthrough: The letter lost is D, the last of Oxford, and it comes off the front of the word for low spirits.
explanation.definitionFit: Throwing someone out, as from a building or a game, is the act of expelling them.

clue.text: First half of prayer for a great painter

definitions.text: First half of prayer for a great painter

blocks.note: surface: the opening part of a prayer
setter's reading: the first PRA, President of the Royal Academy, those being the first three letters of prayer

explanation.surface: Half a prayer said on behalf of a great artist.
explanation.walkthrough: PRA stands for President of the Royal Academy, and the founding president of 1768 was the portrait painter Sir Joshua Reynolds.
explanation.definitionFit: The 18th-century portraitist was the first to head the Royal Academy of Arts, so he is the first PRA and a great painter.

clue.text: Endless task around one part of church

indicators.note: endless means the word loses its final letter
around means the shortened word goes round the next piece

blocks.note: a chore is a routine task
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A never-ending job around one section of a church.
explanation.definitionFit: The choir is the area of a church, near the altar, where the singers sit.

clue.text: Occupy in monastic style

blocks.note: taken as written
a habit is the robe of a monk or nun

explanation.surface: Taking up residence the way monks do.
explanation.definitionFit: To inhabit a place is to live in it, which is to occupy it.

clue.text: Agrees to take in scholar gypsies

indicators.note: taking in means holding something inside, so one word goes within the other

blocks.note: nodding signals agreement
MA is the Master of Arts degree, so a scholar

explanation.surface: Consenting to receive the scholar gypsies of Arnold's poem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scholar gypsies' recalls Matthew Arnold's poem The Scholar-Gipsy, but the two words do different jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: Nomads are wandering people with no fixed home, which is the traditional picture of gypsies.

clue.text: Carefully devised plan for water-supply

blocks.note: first meaning: planned with care
second meaning: a source of water that has been planned

explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning splits the phrase: a well, devised in thought, is a planned water supply.
explanation.definitionFit: Something carefully planned in every detail has been considered fully, and the source of water reading is a pun.

clue.text: She encourages Paddy and Don to go back south

indicators.note: going back means the title is read from its last letter to its first

blocks.note: Pat is a nickname for an Irishman, as Paddy is
Don is a Spanish title for a gentleman, as is senor
S is the abbreviation for south

explanation.surface: A woman cheering on two men called Paddy and Don as they head south again.
explanation.definitionFit: A patroness is a woman who sponsors or supports an artist or cause, so she is one who encourages.

clue.text: Alphabet has one letter different in 24

indicators.note: having one letter different means a single letter of the referenced entry is swapped for another

blocks.note: the answer to 24 down, a town in Surrey

explanation.surface: An alphabet that differs from another by a single letter.
explanation.walkthrough: Change the first letter E of the Surrey town to O.
explanation.definitionFit: Ogham is the ancient Celtic script of strokes cut along the edge of a stone, used for early Irish inscriptions.

clue.text: “And much as Wine has play'd the —” (Fitzgerald)

definitions.text: “And much as Wine has play'd the —” (Fitzgerald)

blocks.clueFragment: “And much as Wine has play'd the —”
blocks.note: a line from FitzGerald's Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam with its last word missing
the poet named so the solver can recall the verse and fill the gap

explanation.walkthrough: FitzGerald's verse runs 'And much as Wine has play'd the Infidel, / And robb'd me of my Robe of Honour'. The gap is the missing word.
explanation.definitionFit: The quotation is completed by the word for an unbeliever, which wine has played by robbing the poet of honour.

clue.text: Be round, ragged and raw

indicators.note: ragged means torn and out of shape, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Advice to be plump, scruffy and sore.
explanation.definitionFit: In the raw means naked, and to be without one's robes is to be undressed.

clue.text: Add to list hospital bed made ready

indicators.note: adding to one word means a further piece is joined on after it

blocks.note: to list is to lean over, as a ship does
H is the abbreviation for hospital

explanation.surface: Put a hospital bed on the list and get it prepared.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface wants a hospital bed; the bed is a garden bed whose soil has been prepared.
explanation.definitionFit: Tilth is soil that has been cultivated and broken up ready for planting, such as a prepared seedbed.

clue.text: Gene's content, in this instance, with a heartless song

indicators.note: without a heart, the word loses its central letter

blocks.note: here means in this case
a ditty is a short simple song

explanation.surface: A gene's contents, here illustrated with a soulless song.
explanation.walkthrough: The song has four letters around its middle T; take one of the pair of Ts out as the heart.
explanation.definitionFit: What genes carry is the passing on of traits from parents to offspring, the biological inheritance.

clue.text: Decline several years as soon as love goes

indicators.note: goes means departs, so that letter leaves the phrase

blocks.note: a decade is ten years
once means as soon as, as in once you arrive
O is a zero, love in tennis

explanation.surface: Years of decline that start as soon as love departs.
explanation.walkthrough: Love is O, the zero score in tennis; remove it from the word for as soon as.
explanation.definitionFit: Decadence is moral or cultural decay, a falling away from former standards.

clue.text: Hirsute spirit without beard — not bad!

indicators.note: not here means the following letters are taken out of the word before
without means outside, so the spirit goes round the other piece

blocks.note: whisky is a spirit
taken as written
taken as written, to be removed

explanation.surface: A hairy spirit, with a beard that is not half bad.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the letters of bad out of beard to leave two letters, and put them inside the spirit.
explanation.definitionFit: Whiskery describes having whiskers, so it means hairy, which is what hirsute means.

clue.text: Plant about a hundred

indicators.note: about means going round, so the hundred surrounds the single letter

blocks.note: taken as written
a century is a hundred

explanation.surface: A plant numbering roughly a hundred.
explanation.definitionFit: Centaury is a small herb of the gentian family with pink flowers, once used medicinally.

clue.text: Earnest, if devious, oriental

indicators.note: devious means winding and indirect, so the letters take a crooked path

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone sincere yet sly, from the Orient.
explanation.definitionFit: Eastern means from or of the East, which is what oriental means.

clue.text: Round out after this

blocks.note: first meaning: a round sung by several voices, often comic
second meaning: in cricket a batsman is out when the ball is caught

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a batsman is dismissed if a fielder takes the ball before it bounces.
explanation.definitionFit: A catch is both a musical round for voices and the taking of a hit ball that dismisses the batsman.

clue.text: Capital decoration for highest speed on water

blocks.note: top means highest
a knot is a unit of speed at sea

explanation.surface: An ornament on the top of a column awarded for record speed on water.
explanation.walkthrough: Capital here means of the head, not a city or a column top.
explanation.definitionFit: A topknot is a ribbon or tuft of hair on top of the head, so it is an ornament for the head.

clue.text: Figure task's not started — yearn to finish it

indicators.note: not started means the word has lost its opening letter

blocks.note: a job is a task
to long is to yearn

explanation.surface: A shape-drawing job left unbegun, with a longing to complete it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To finish it' places the yearning word at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: An oblong is a rectangle longer than it is wide, a geometric figure.

clue.text: Beg a bit of bread and cheese spread

indicators.note: a bit of a word is a small piece of it, here its opening letter
spread suggests scattering, so the letters are laid out in new order

blocks.note: the opening letter of bread
the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Pleading for a morsel of bread and a cheese spread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheese spread' reads as a single food; 'spread' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To beseech is to ask earnestly or implore, the same as to beg.

clue.text: For instance, one who survived the flood near Runnymede

definitions.note: describes a place, not a synonym

blocks.note: e.g. abbreviates for example
Ham was a son of Noah who lived through the Flood in the Ark

explanation.surface: An example of a flood survivor living near Runnymede.
explanation.walkthrough: Runnymede, by the Thames, is where Magna Carta was sealed; the town beside it floods often.
explanation.definitionFit: Egham is a Surrey town on the Thames immediately next to the meadow of Runnymede.

clue.text: Complex rex

blocks.note: surface: a complicated king
setter's reading: the name that comes before both Complex and Rex, in Freud and in Sophocles

explanation.walkthrough: Freud's complex and Sophocles' play 'Rex' both carry the same Theban king's name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek king who unknowingly married his mother gives his name to Freud's complex and to Sophocles' tragedy.

clue.text: Once held by some to be a Haitian ritual

indicators.note: held by some of the words means the letters sit inside a run of them

blocks.note: the run of letters across these words

explanation.surface: A Haitian ceremony that some people used to believe in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Haitian' looks part of the definition but supplies the last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Obeah is a form of folk magic and sorcery practised in the West Indies.

clue.text: Decree one in arms ...

indicators.note: in means placed inside the following word

blocks.note: ordnance means military weapons and supplies
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: An order putting someone under arms, leading into the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: An ordinance is an authoritative order or a local regulation, which is a decree.

clue.text: ... got from him, stung him, possibly

definitions.note: with the previous clue: one from whom arms are got

indicators.note: possibly signals the letters could be arranged another way

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Continuing the last clue: arms obtained from a man, who perhaps got stung.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis carries 'arms' over from 27: the definition is arms got from him.
explanation.definitionFit: A gunsmith makes and sells firearms, so he is the person weapons are bought from.

clue.text: Ecstatic railway guard

blocks.note: sent means transported with delight
RY is an abbreviation for railway

explanation.surface: A thrilled guard on a train.
explanation.definitionFit: A sentry is a soldier posted to keep watch, which is a guard.
